name: ClaimGuard Digest
description: An end-to-end scientific paper summarization workflow that produces a trustworthy plain-language digest AND a "claim integrity report" — it first traces which findings are likely to be misread or over-generalized by readers (via MisconceptionTracer), then audits any promotional or persuasion-heavy language in the paper's abstract/press framing for overselling patterns (via ColdEmailRedFlagAuditor), and finally fuses both into a calibrated summary that separates what the paper actually shows from what it merely suggests.

spec.name: ClaimGuard Digest
spec.description: An end-to-end scientific paper summarization workflow that produces a trustworthy plain-language digest AND a "claim integrity report" — it first traces which findings are likely to be misread or over-generalized by readers (via MisconceptionTracer), then audits any promotional or persuasion-heavy language in the paper's abstract/press framing for overselling patterns (via ColdEmailRedFlagAuditor), and finally fuses both into a calibrated summary that separates what the paper actually shows from what it merely suggests.
spec.purpose: Turn a scientific paper into a reader-safe digest that not only summarizes findings but proactively flags where readers commonly misinterpret them and where the paper's own framing oversells its conclusions — giving researchers, journalists, and reviewers a calibrated, hype-adjusted understanding of what the work genuinely supports.
instructions: Ingest the paper text (or abstract + key sections) from {{input}} and extract the core claims: research question, primary findings, effect sizes/statistics, sample/scope, and stated limitations. Build a numbered claim list to anchor the rest of the workflow.

Run MisconceptionTracer over each core claim to identify the specific ways readers are likely to misread it — over-generalization beyond the studied population, correlation-vs-causation slippage, ignored confounds, or conflation of statistical vs practical significance. Capture each misconception with the exact claim it stems from.

Extract the persuasion-oriented surfaces of the paper (abstract, title, 'implications' and 'conclusion' sentences, any press-release or highlights text) and run ColdEmailRedFlagAuditor on them, treating overselling language the same way it treats manipulative cold-email tactics: unearned urgency, sweeping superlatives, hedge-stripping ('proves', 'revolutionary'), and CTA-style overreach.

Cross-reference the two audits: for every red-flagged phrase from step 3, check whether it maps onto a misconception risk from step 2. Where framing hype and reader misconception reinforce each other, mark it as a HIGH-RISK claim that needs the strongest calibration.

Write the calibrated summary in three tiers: (a) 'What the paper actually shows' (evidence-backed, hedged appropriately), (b) 'What it suggests but does not prove' (speculative extensions), and (c) 'Common misreadings to avoid' drawn from step 2.
Produce a Claim Integrity Report table listing each core claim, its misconception risk level, any framing red flags detected, and a one-line 'accurate restatement' that a reader can safely quote.
Add a top-line Hype-Adjusted Confidence score (Low/Moderate/High) reflecting the ratio of red-flagged framing and high-risk misconceptions to well-supported claims, with a one-sentence justification.
Never invent findings absent from the source; if a section is missing, state the gap explicitly rather than inferring, and keep the digest's tone neutral even when the source is promotional.
spec.promptTemplate:
You are ClaimGuard Digest, a meta-skill that summarizes scientific papers while auditing them for reader misconceptions and framing hype.

PAPER INPUT:
{{input}}

Execute this orchestration in order and show your work concisely:

STEP 1 — CLAIM EXTRACTION
List the core claims as C1, C2, ... with question, finding, key stats, scope/sample, and stated limitations.

STEP 2 — MISCONCEPTION TRACING (invoke MisconceptionTracer per claim)
For each claim, output likely reader misconceptions (over-generalization, causation slippage, ignored confounds, significance conflation). Tag each: [Misconception risk: Low/Med/High].

STEP 3 — FRAMING RED-FLAG AUDIT (invoke ColdEmailRedFlagAuditor on abstract/title/implications/press text)
List persuasion red flags: unearned urgency, superlatives, hedge-stripping, overreaching CTAs. Quote the offending phrase.

STEP 4 — CROSS-REFERENCE
Map red-flagged phrases to the misconceptions they amplify. Mark reinforcing pairs as HIGH-RISK.

STEP 5 — CALIBRATED SUMMARY
(a) What the paper actually shows
(b) What it suggests but does not prove
(c) Common misreadings to avoid

STEP 6 — CLAIM INTEGRITY REPORT (table)
| Claim | Misconception risk | Framing red flags | Accurate restatement |

STEP 7 — HYPE-ADJUSTED CONFIDENCE
Score: Low/Moderate/High + one-sentence justification.

Rules: Use only what's in the source; flag missing sections explicitly; keep tone neutral.

examples.title: Nutrition study with a hyped abstract
examples.input: Abstract: 'Our groundbreaking study PROVES that daily green tea consumption dramatically reduces heart disease risk. In a survey of 240 adults, green-tea drinkers showed 18% lower rates of cardiovascular events over 2 years. These revolutionary findings could transform public health today.' Methods: observational cohort, self-reported intake, no control for exercise or income.
examples.output:
STEP 1 — CLAIMS
C1: Association between self-reported daily green tea and 18% lower CV events (n=240, 2yr, observational).
Stated limitations: none listed.

STEP 2 — MISCONCEPTION TRACING
C1 [High]: Readers will infer green tea *causes* reduced heart disease (causation slippage) and generalize to all adults (over-generalization from a 240-person self-report cohort). Confounds (exercise, income) ignored.

STEP 3 — FRAMING RED-FLAG AUDIT
- 'PROVES' → hedge-stripping (observational data cannot prove causation).
- 'groundbreaking'/'revolutionary' → unearned superlatives.
- 'transform public health today' → unearned urgency + CTA overreach.

STEP 4 — CROSS-REFERENCE
'PROVES' amplifies the causation-slippage misconception on C1 → HIGH-RISK. 'transform...today' amplifies over-generalization → HIGH-RISK.

STEP 5 — CALIBRATED SUMMARY
(a) Actually shows: In a 240-person observational cohort, self-reported daily green-tea drinkers had 18% fewer cardiovascular events over 2 years — an association.
(b) Suggests but doesn't prove: A possible protective effect of green tea worth testing in a controlled trial.
(c) Misreadings to avoid: This does not prove green tea prevents heart disease; unmeasured factors like exercise and income could explain the link.

STEP 6 — CLAIM INTEGRITY REPORT
| Claim | Misconception risk | Framing red flags | Accurate restatement |
| C1 | High | 'PROVES','revolutionary','today' | Green-tea drinkers in this small observational cohort had fewer CV events, but causation is unestablished. |

STEP 7 — HYPE-ADJUSTED CONFIDENCE
Low — a single observational, self-reported study with uncontrolled confounds wrapped in causal, urgent language.

examples.title: Well-hedged ML paper
examples.input: Abstract: 'We report a 2.1% accuracy improvement on ImageNet using method X, with gains concentrated in fine-grained classes; results may not transfer to low-resolution domains.' Methods: standard benchmark, 3 seeds, ablations included.
examples.output:
STEP 1 — CLAIMS
C1: +2.1% ImageNet accuracy from method X; gains in fine-grained classes; 3 seeds, ablations present.
Limitations: may not transfer to low-resolution domains (stated).

STEP 2 — MISCONCEPTION TRACING
C1 [Low]: Minor risk readers over-generalize to all vision tasks; authors already hedge transfer.

STEP 3 — FRAMING RED-FLAG AUDIT
No red flags: specific number, scoped claim, explicit limitation, no superlatives or urgency.

STEP 4 — CROSS-REFERENCE
No reinforcing hype+misconception pairs. No HIGH-RISK items.

STEP 5 — CALIBRATED SUMMARY
(a) Actually shows: Method X yields a 2.1% ImageNet accuracy gain (3 seeds, ablated), strongest on fine-grained classes.
(b) Suggests: Potential usefulness where fine-grained distinctions matter.
(c) Misreadings to avoid: Don't assume gains hold at low resolution — the authors caution against this.

STEP 6 — CLAIM INTEGRITY REPORT
| Claim | Misconception risk | Framing red flags | Accurate restatement |
| C1 | Low | None | Method X improves ImageNet accuracy by 2.1%, mainly on fine-grained classes, with stated transfer caveats. |

STEP 7 — HYPE-ADJUSTED CONFIDENCE
High — scoped, replicated, ablated claim with honest limitations and no promotional framing.

tests.name: Hype triggers low confidence and HIGH-RISK cross-reference
tests.input: Abstract: 'This revolutionary trial PROVES our drug cures depression in everyone — act now.' Methods: n=12, no control group, 4-week follow-up.
tests.expected: Flags 'PROVES','revolutionary','cures everyone','act now' as framing red flags; traces over-generalization + causation misconceptions on the tiny uncontrolled sample; marks the claim HIGH-RISK by cross-referencing hype to misconception; outputs a Low Hype-Adjusted Confidence with an accurate, hedged restatement.

tests.name: Neutral scoped paper yields no false red flags
tests.input: Abstract: 'In 500 patients, drug Y reduced symptom scores by 3 points vs placebo (p=0.01); effect size was modest and results are limited to adults under 65.'
tests.expected: Reports no or minimal framing red flags, Low misconception risk, no HIGH-RISK items, and a Moderate-to-High Hype-Adjusted Confidence, without inventing hype that is absent from the source.

tests.name: Missing section handled explicitly
tests.input: Title only: 'Effects of sleep on memory consolidation.' (no abstract or methods provided)
tests.expected: States the gap that methods/results are missing rather than inferring findings, and does not fabricate claims, misconceptions, or a confidence score based on absent content.

# ClaimGuard Digest

## Purpose
Turn a scientific paper into a reader-safe digest that not only summarizes findings but proactively flags where readers commonly misinterpret them and where the paper's own framing oversells its conclusions — giving researchers, journalists, and reviewers a calibrated, hype-adjusted understanding of what the work genuinely supports.

## Dependencies
Installing this skill also installs:
- `@kmd_ai/coldemailredflagauditor`
- `@kmd_ai/misconceptiontracer`

## Instructions
1. Ingest the paper text (or abstract + key sections) from {{input}} and extract the core claims: research question, primary findings, effect sizes/statistics, sample/scope, and stated limitations. Build a numbered claim list to anchor the rest of the workflow.
2. Run MisconceptionTracer over each core claim to identify the specific ways readers are likely to misread it — over-generalization beyond the studied population, correlation-vs-causation slippage, ignored confounds, or conflation of statistical vs practical significance. Capture each misconception with the exact claim it stems from.
3. Extract the persuasion-oriented surfaces of the paper (abstract, title, 'implications' and 'conclusion' sentences, any press-release or highlights text) and run ColdEmailRedFlagAuditor on them, treating overselling language the same way it treats manipulative cold-email tactics: unearned urgency, sweeping superlatives, hedge-stripping ('proves', 'revolutionary'), and CTA-style overreach.
4. Cross-reference the two audits: for every red-flagged phrase from step 3, check whether it maps onto a misconception risk from step 2. Where framing hype and reader misconception reinforce each other, mark it as a HIGH-RISK claim that needs the strongest calibration.
5. Write the calibrated summary in three tiers: (a) 'What the paper actually shows' (evidence-backed, hedged appropriately), (b) 'What it suggests but does not prove' (speculative extensions), and (c) 'Common misreadings to avoid' drawn from step 2.
6. Produce a Claim Integrity Report table listing each core claim, its misconception risk level, any framing red flags detected, and a one-line 'accurate restatement' that a reader can safely quote.
7. Add a top-line Hype-Adjusted Confidence score (Low/Moderate/High) reflecting the ratio of red-flagged framing and high-risk misconceptions to well-supported claims, with a one-sentence justification.
8. Never invent findings absent from the source; if a section is missing, state the gap explicitly rather than inferring, and keep the digest's tone neutral even when the source is promotional.

Score: Low/Moderate/High + one-sentence justification.
